# Summary: Liberal Democrats 1997 Manifesto - "Make the Difference"

## Overview and Vision
The Liberal Democrats presented their 1997 manifesto as a programme to modernise Britain, emphasising liberty, equality, and community. Leader Paddy Ashdown argued that 18 years of Conservative government had left society divided, public services underfunded, and the economy underperforming. The party positioned itself as willing to make difficult choices other parties avoided.

## Education: The Top Priority
Education was the manifesto's centrepiece, with a commitment to invest an additional £2 billion annually, funded by raising income tax by 1p. Key pledges included providing early years education for all 3-4 year olds, doubling spending on school books and equipment, reducing primary class sizes to maximum 30 pupils, and tackling building repairs. The party proposed scrapping the voucher scheme, establishing a General Teaching Council, and creating Individual Learning Accounts for lifelong learning.

## Economic Policy
The Liberal Democrats advocated economic stability through making the Bank of England independent, keeping inflation low, and potentially joining the European single currency (subject to meeting criteria and a referendum). They proposed supporting small businesses through better finance access, reducing red tape, and establishing regional Development Agencies. A key innovation was shifting taxation from employment to pollution and resource depletion.

## Environment
Environmental protection featured prominently, with targets to cut carbon dioxide emissions by 30% over 15 years. Proposals included a National Homes Insulation programme, a "carbon tax" on fossil fuels (offset by cuts to VAT and employers' National Insurance), investment in public transport, trebling rail freight, and reforming car taxation to favour fuel-efficient vehicles.

## Crime and Housing
The manifesto pledged 3,000 more police officers on the beat, tackling youth crime through community repayment schemes, and ending rough sleeping by 2000. Housing proposals included building more affordable homes, introducing Mortgage Benefit for first-time buyers, and bringing empty properties back into use.

## NHS and Welfare
Healthcare commitments included an extra £540 million annually, halting finance-driven hospital closures, recruiting 10,000 additional nurses or 5,000 doctors, cutting waiting lists to six months maximum, and restoring free eye and dental checks. The party proposed modernising welfare through a Benefit Transfer Programme helping long-term unemployed into work and breaking poverty traps by raising tax thresholds.

## Constitutional Reform
Major democratic reforms included proportional representation for all elections, a Bill of Rights incorporating the European Convention on Human Rights, Freedom of Information legislation, Home Rule for Scotland and Wales with their own parliaments, reducing MPs by one-third, and transforming the House of Lords into a predominantly elected chamber.

## Europe and Foreign Policy
The party advocated positive European engagement, supporting participation in a successful single currency, making EU institutions more democratic, and enlarging Europe to include eastern democracies. Defence commitments included maintaining Trident (with reduced warheads), strengthening NATO, and reforming the United Nations.

## Funding Commitments
The manifesto was presented as "a menu with prices," with specific funding sources identified: 1p income tax rise for education, a new 50p tax rate on income over £100,000 (funding tax threshold increases), and 5p on cigarettes for NHS improvements. The party pledged that 70% of adults would pay lower or unchanged income tax.
